content.text:
VERDICT: CHANGES REQUESTED

The refactor is otherwise clean and well-executed: `IdentityKey` correctly delegates hashing to the existing `Hashes.sha256Hex` and phonetics to the new `Soundex`, the three consumers (`RequireUniqueIdentity`, `AssignOwnerPossibleDuplicate`, mapper) all key off the one shared definition, and every javadoc — including `HouseholdKey`'s "no longer keys off the household id" note — was updated coherently. No catch-all classes, no logic misplaced into a function step, and the "single definition of X … kept out of function classes" doc idiom is followed faithfully.

One structural finding:

**`Soundex` is in the wrong package — it belongs in `function/common`, not `function/owner`.**

`Soundex` is a pure, domain-agnostic, standard string algorithm. It encodes no owner policy whatsoever — it takes a name and returns a phonetic code. This is exactly the shape of `Luhn` (a standard checksum algorithm) and `Hashes` (SHA-256 hex), both of which this codebase deliberately places in `function/common`. Notably, `Luhn` is used *only* by owner-domain code (`CustomerCode`) yet still lives in `common` — so "single current consumer is in owner" is not this codebase's reason for owner-package placement. The established convention is: generic reusable algorithms → `common`; owner-domain policy helpers (`TelephoneNormalizer`'s E.164 rules, `EmailNormalizer`, `HouseholdKey`, `IdentityKey`) → `owner`.

`Soundex` sits on the wrong side of that line. It reads like a sibling of `Luhn`, and `IdentityKey` already imports `Hashes` from `common`, so importing `Soundex` from there too would be natural. Concretely:
- Move `Soundex` to `org.springframework.samples.petclinic.rest.function.common`.
- Make it `public` (like `Luhn`/`Hashes`) and add the `import` in `IdentityKey` / `AssignOwnerPossibleDuplicate`.
- Its "Kept out of the function classes … one public method" javadoc note can be dropped, matching `Luhn`/`Hashes`, which omit it since it only makes sense for the owner-package helpers that neighbor function classes.

This keeps the "generic algorithm in `common`" precedent intact so a maintainer looking for reusable string utilities finds them all in one place.
